name: blockchain-based
context: Multi-party systems requiring trustless consensus, immutable audit trails, and decentralized control without a trusted intermediary
benefits: Immutability: Records cannot be altered retroactively after consensus
Transparency: All participants can verify transactions on shared ledger
Decentralization: No single point of control or failure
Trust minimization: Eliminates need for trusted intermediary between parties
Programmability: Smart contracts automate business logic execution
Cryptographic integrity: Hash chaining ensures data integrity
Multi-party consensus: Agreement without central authority
tradeoffs: Scalability limitations: Limited transaction throughput (3-7k TPS vs 50k+ for traditional DBs)
Higher latency: Consensus and confirmation take significant time
Storage growth: Ledger grows indefinitely, requiring pruning strategies
Complexity: Cryptographic key management and wallet infrastructure
Energy consumption: PoW consensus is energy intensive (mitigated by PoS)
Cost overhead: Consensus mechanism has inherent computational cost
Data sensitivity: Immutable ledger conflicts with GDPR right to erasure
Irreversibility: Corrections require complex hard fork or offset transactions
use_cases: Multi-party trust requirements where parties don't trust each other
Need for immutable, tamper-proof audit trail
Cross-organization data sharing without central authority
Smart contract automation for conditional asset transfers
Financial settlement and reconciliation between institutions
Voting systems requiring transparency and verifiability
avoid_when: Single organization with no multi-party trust requirements
Data frequently needs correction or deletion
Simple state with no automation or trust requirements
Internal systems only with trusted parties
Strong consistency requirements within single database
component_types: Distributed Ledger: Shared record of transactions replicated across all nodes
Consensus Layer: Protocol for agreeing on ledger state (PoW, PoS, PBFT)
Smart Contract Engine: Runtime for executing self-executing code on blockchain
Peer-to-Peer Network: Nodes communicate directly without central server
Cryptographic Layer: SHA-256/Keccak hashing ensures data integrity and block linkage
Merkle Tree Verifier: Efficient verification of transaction data within blocks
Wallet/Key Management: Cryptographic key storage and transaction signing
Node Client: Software client that participates in the blockchain network
anti_patterns: Blockchain for blockchain's sake: using when centralized solution suffices
On-chain storage of large datasets: use off-chain with on-chain hashes
Putting PII on immutable ledger: violates GDPR and data privacy
Single-organization blockchain: centralized control defeats purpose
Ignoring gas/transaction fees in design: costs accumulate rapidly
Overly complex smart contracts: audit difficulty and reentrancy risks
design_principles: Cryptographic Integrity: All transactions must be digitally signed and hash-chained to ensure data integrity
Decentralization First: Avoid single points of control; distribute trust across multiple participants
Immutability by Design: Once consensus is reached, records cannot be altered; design for append-only patterns
Trustless Verification: No participant must trust another; all claims are verifiable through consensus
Minimal On-Chain Data: Store only essential data on-chain; use off-chain storage for large datasets
Formal Verification: Smart contracts should undergo formal verification before deployment
Defense in Depth: Implement multiple security layers; assume any component can be compromised
Privacy by Default: Design assuming data will be visible to all participants; use encryption where needed
best_practices: Start Small: Pilot with document verification or supply chain tracking before full deployment
Off-Chain Sensitive Data: Personal data cannot live on immutable ledgers per GDPR; use off-chain storage with on-chain hashes
Hybrid Architectures: Keep operational data in legacy systems, anchor proofs on-chain for verifiability
Abstract Blockchain Specifics: Create isolation layers for future platform migration
Design for Interoperability: Consider Hyperledger Cacti, Chainlink CCIP for cross-chain communication
Implement Robust Key Management: Use hardware security modules (HSMs) for production key storage
Plan for Governance: Establish clear decision-making processes before network launch
Monitor Gas/Transaction Costs: Design for cost predictability; batch operations when possible
Use Modular Architecture: Separate concerns to allow technology upgrades without full redesign
